question: Why does list.map((item, i) => <Item key={i} />) cause performance issues when the list is reordered? Why is a stable key better?
options: Index key breaks identity; reordering items makes React think they changed, state/focus misalign
Index key is optimal for list performance
Key doesn't affect list rendering
Stable keys cause more re-renders
explanation: Index keys tie component identity to position, not content; reordering shifts indices, making React think item A is now B, losing component state and focus.

question: Why does React batch multiple setState calls into one re-render in React 18? setState(1); setState(2); setState(3);
options: Batching reduces render work; all updates commit once, not three times
No batching, each setState causes re-render
Batching only works in event handlers
Batching is automatic in React 16
explanation: React 18 batches all updates in event handlers, effects, and microtasks; one re-render commits all queued state changes, reducing browser work.

question: Given a component with expensive render, why might React.memo() not improve performance? const Memo = React.memo(Component); <Memo x={obj} />
options: memo's shallow equality fails if obj reference changed; new object every render = always re-render
memo always skips re-renders
memo has no performance benefit
Component re-renders are unavoidable
explanation: memo compares props with ===; if props.x is a new object every render (like { ... }), memo sees 'change' and re-renders anyway.

question: Why might useMemo(() => expensiveCompute(), [x, y]) cause stale results if dependencies are missing?
options: Missing dependencies mean memo doesn't re-compute; stale result persists even if dependency changed
Dependencies are optional, memo always re-computes
useMemo doesn't memoize
stale results are impossible
explanation: useMemo returns cached result if dependencies haven't changed; missing a dependency means the old result is returned even if inputs changed.

question: Given a large list with 1000 items, why is virtualization (rendering only visible items) more performant?
options: Rendering 1000 items creates 1000 DOM nodes; virtualizing renders only 20 visible, reducing work
Virtualization is not faster
Virtualization is only for mobile
All items must be rendered for performance
explanation: Virtualization renders only visible items; as user scrolls, old items unmount and new ones mount, keeping DOM small and fast.

question: Why might breaking one large component into smaller components improve performance? const Big = () => { ... lots of state ... }
options: Smaller components re-render independently; one component's state change doesn't force all descendants to re-render
Component size doesn't affect performance
Large components are always faster
Splitting components increases re-renders
explanation: Splitting components creates independent re-render boundaries; child components only re-render if their own state/props change, not parent state.

question: Why does useCallback(() => { ... }, []) without dependencies create a stale-closure trap for performance?
options: Empty deps cache old closure forever; passing stale values to children defeats memo()
useCallback auto-updates dependencies
Empty deps always give current values
useCallback doesn't affect performance
explanation: Empty deps cache the callback with old closure values; even though the callback reference stays same (memo passes), it uses stale data.

question: Why might debouncing or throttling a fast onChange handler improve performance? const [search, setSearch] = useState('');
options: Debouncing delays updates, reducing re-renders from every keystroke
All keystrokes must update state immediately
Debouncing prevents state updates
Keystroke speed doesn't affect performance
explanation: Debouncing delays setState until typing stops; instead of re-rendering on every keystroke, it batches updates, reducing render work.

question: Given Suspense with React.lazy, why does lazy loading improve performance? const Lazy = lazy(() => import('./Component'));
options: Lazy loading defers bundle download until component is used, reducing initial bundle size
Lazy loading has no performance benefit
lazy() requires network requests
Suspense and lazy are unrelated
explanation: lazy() uses dynamic import; the module is only bundled/downloaded when the component is first rendered, reducing initial page load time.

question: Why might code-splitting by route (instead of one large bundle) improve time-to-interactive? <Route path='/dashboard' component={lazy(() => import('./Dashboard'))} />
options: Smaller initial bundle loads faster, user sees app quicker; other routes load on demand
Code-splitting has no impact on load time
One large bundle is always better
Routes must share a bundle
explanation: Splitting by route means initial bundle contains only home/login; dashboard and other routes are loaded when navigated to, reducing time-to-interactive.
